newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu faces difficult home-coming. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu faces difficult home-coming. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]

text.p: If Zaire's ailing president, Mobutu Sese Seko, returns home this week as promised, he will face one of his biggest challenges in over three decades in power.

With Tutsi-led rebels in the east talking of marching to Kinshasa to depose him, Mobutu, 66 (corrects age), may have to dig deep into his store of political acumen to maintain his hold on the sprawling and anarchic Central African nation.

Allies and some opponents welcome his homecoming after cancer surgery and prolonged convalescence in Europe but opinions vary widely as to just what he will do and whether it will help or just make matters worse.

"It will give us the electro-shock we need," Banza Mukalayi, Mobutu's number two in the People's Revolutionary Movement (MPR), told Reuters at the weekend. "President Mobutu is the symbol of Zaire's unity and territorial integrity and his return will put us back on the offensive," he added.
But sceptics say Mobutu is in no position either politically or physically to pull magic solutions out of his trademark leopard-skin hat.

"The rebellion in the east is like the AIDS virus. It has invaded our defence system and made it vulnerable to all kinds of diseases," one opposition legislator from the eastern town of Kisangani told Reuters. "I, for one, do not expect Mr Mobutu to provide a miraculous cure."
Senior presidential aides say Mobutu, who has dominated Zaire's political life since seizing power in 1965, will fly home from France on Tuesday or Wednesday.

Mobutu had prostate surgery in August. The revolt in the east broke out on October 18. The Rwandan-backed rebels routed Zaire's poorly trained and demoralised army, capturing the major eastern border towns of Goma and Bukavu.

The rebel thrust put hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees to flight. Many, despite fears of reprisals for the 1994 genocide of up to a million minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners, have since returned to Rwanda.
Mobutu's illness has brought seething political tensions to the surface, prompting speculation that Africa's third largest nation would tear itself apart without him.
Supporters say the return of Mobutu, who hopes to contest elections which must be held by July 1997, will solder its disparate regions back together.

Allies and long-time foes say Mobutu should use his influence to reinstate radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi as prime minister at the head of a national unity government. Tshisekedi hinted as much would happen after "reconciliation" talks with Mobutu in France in November.

Constitutionally, Mobutu, who bowed to foreign and domestic pressure for democratic reform in 1990, has no power to change government or the military high command without the support of the transitional parliament or the cooperation of ministers.
His supporters are in a majority in parliament and in the past he has not shied away from using his position to make or break political allies or opponents.
But Banza Mukalayi says the relationship cuts both ways. "He can change our opinion just as we can change his," he said.
If talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila are to be an option, as Tshisekedi has suggested, that relationship could prove crucial -- Mobutu's supporters fiercely oppose talks.
Government officials fear Mobutu may oust centrist Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who has done much to clean up Zaire's corruption-plagued economy, and reinstate Tshisekedi.
Tshisekedi has laid claim to the job since Mobutu shunted him aside in 1993 in favour of an appointee of his own.
"That way Tshisekedi will inherit an impossible situation and the people will see he is no more capable of solving their problems than anyone else," the government official said.
As commander in chief of the armed force, Mobutu's return is expected to provide a psychological boost to the army.

"The problems in the high command are problems within Mobutu's own clan and family. He knows better than anyone how to deal with this," a senior presidential aide said. "He is in a position to install a leadership based on military merit."
Members of the officer class agree but opponents blame three decades of Mobutu rule for Zaire's problems.

"The situation we are living now is a consequence of Mobutu's politics," said Doctor Jean Baptiste Sondji, a surgeon at the crumbling Mama Yemo hospital and a founding member of the radical Patriotic Front.
"If the army is dislocated now it is because Mobutu never trusted it. I think his return will only complicate matters."
